newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan sets stage for rate increase next week.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan sets stage for rate increase next week.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan set the stage on Thursday for an increase in interest rates next week, stressing the importance of prompt action to keep inflation down before it hurts the economy.
In testimony to the Joint Economic Committee of Congress, he said the economy retains a "great deal of vigor" and called the prospects for a continued upswing "quite favourable."
The central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Tuesday to consider raising short-term rates for the first time in over two years.

"Should we choose to alter monetary policy, we know from past experience that, although the financial markets may respond immediately, the main effects on inflationary pressures may not be felt until late this year and in 1998," Greenspan said.

Stock prices fell as Greenspan's remarks heightened expectations on Wall Street for a rise in short-term rates next week. The Dow Jones industrial average of blue chip shares closed 57.40 points lower at 6,820.28.
Higher rates would slow the economy and prevent higher inflation, but would also crimp corporate profits by raising borrowing costs for consumers and companies.
Much of Greenspan's testimony seemed aimed at preparing lawmakers -- who have often been critical of Fed policy in the past -- for the possibility of a rate increase next week.

Pressed by Committee Chairman Jim Saxton to explain why the Fed was weighing higher rates now when inflation was low, Greenspan retorted that the central bank needed to look ahead to anticipate price pressures in the future.

"What we at the Federal Open Market Committee are going to have to judge ... is not so much the question of where prices are or have been, but rather what is the state of the economy later this year and into 1998," he told the New Jersey House Republican.
Greenspan saw upward pressure on underlying inflation this year as the labour market remains tight, encouraging workers to demand higher wages and companies to pay them.

So far, the tight job market has not led to higher inflation. Worried about losing their jobs, workers have held back from pushing for excessive pay hikes, while companies have been forced to keep prices down by competition.

But Greenspan made clear that could only last so long and said that a further drop in the unemployment rate ran the risk of higher wages leading to faster inflation. The unemployment rate is now 5.3 percent, just above an eight-year low.

The Fed has not changed interest rates since Jan. 31, 1996, when it cut them by a quarter percentage point as insurance against an economic slowdown. The central bank last raised short-term rates on Feb. 1, 1995.

The central bank's target for the federal funds rate -- the rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans -- is 5.25 percent. The discount rate -- the rate that the Fed charges on its loans to the banks -- is 5 percent.

At their meeting on Tuesday, Fed policy-makers will have to judge whether the strong pace of the economic expansion will continue and what impact that might eventually have on inflation, Greenspan said.
"Activity has retained a great deal of vigour in early 1997," the central bank chief said. "The prospects for sustaining the expansion are quite favourable."
Flush with higher wages and investment gains from the stock market, consumers look likely to keep on spending at a solid clip, he added.

But he steered clear of any specific comments on the stock market. Greenspan rocked global markets in December and again last month when he suggested that equity prices might be too high as a result of what he called investors' irrational exuberance.
